explanation: SET NOCOUNT OFF leaves row-count (DONE_IN_PROC) messages enabled for every statement in usp_TestProcedure, adding client/network chatter.
SET XACT_ABORT OFF while the procedure uses explicit transactions (lines 181 and 238) lets run-time errors leave a transaction open and partially applied instead of aborting automatically.
SELECT * returns every current and future column of Sales.Orders, wasting bandwidth and breaking callers when the schema changes.
TOP (10) without ORDER BY returns an arbitrary set of 10 orders; the result is nondeterministic across executions.
DISTINCT on o.OrderID is redundant because OrderID is the primary key of Sales.Orders; it adds a needless duplicate-elimination sort/aggregate.
WITH (NOLOCK) on Sales.Orders permits dirty reads, missing rows, and duplicated rows during page splits.
YEAR(o.OrderDate) wraps the filtered OrderDate column in a function, preventing a range seek; use explicit date boundaries instead.
o.CustomerID (int) is compared with @CustomerIdText (nvarchar(20)); SQL Server implicitly converts the string side, risking conversion errors and degraded cardinality estimates.
The @CustomerID IS NULL OR o.CustomerID = @CustomerID pattern prevents a stable seek plan and tends to scan Sales.Orders for every parameter value.
LIKE N'%urgent%' begins with a wildcard, so the Comments predicate cannot use an index seek and scans Sales.Orders.
NOT IN (SELECT i.CustomerID FROM Sales.Invoices) returns no rows at all if the subquery ever produces a NULL; NOT EXISTS gives null-safe anti-join semantics.
ISNULL(o.CustomerID, 0) = 1 wraps the indexed CustomerID column, making the predicate non-sargable; CustomerID is NOT NULL so the wrapper is also unnecessary.
o.OrderID + 0 performs arithmetic on the key column in the predicate, blocking a direct index seek on PK_Sales_Orders.
o.CustomerID <> 1 is an inequality that typically scans most of Sales.Orders rather than seeking a narrow range.
CROSS JOIN between Sales.Orders and Sales.Customers has no join predicate, multiplying Orders by Customers before TOP (1) picks an arbitrary row.
Comma-separated tables in FROM with the join condition in WHERE is legacy syntax; use an explicit INNER JOIN between Orders and OrderLines.
The correlated COUNT(*) subquery against Sales.OrderLines is evaluated once per outer order row; a grouped join or OUTER APPLY would be set-based.
The correlated EXISTS probe into Sales.OrderLines runs per outer row; expressing it as a set-based semi-join lets the optimizer pick a better plan.
The CASE WHEN o.Comments IS NULL THEN 0 ELSE 1 END expression is duplicated in the select list and ORDER BY, inviting drift and repeated evaluation.
ORDER BY 2 sorts by select-list position; reordering the columns silently changes the sort key.
OFFSET/FETCH orders only by non-unique o.OrderDate, so rows can repeat or be skipped between pages; add OrderID as a stable tie-breaker.
UNION between the OrderID = 1 and OrderID = 2 branches is already disjoint; the duplicate-elimination work is wasted and UNION ALL should be used.
(SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Sales.OrderLines ...) > 0 counts every matching line when EXISTS would stop at the first match.
SELECT @OrderID = o.OrderID FROM Sales.Orders assigns from an unordered multi-row set; the value kept depends on plan order and silently discards all other rows.
The @OrderIds table variable has no statistics and is estimated at one row on older compatibility levels, producing poor plans when populated from Sales.Orders.
SELECT ... INTO #ImplicitOrders creates the temp-table schema implicitly and can hold schema locks; declare the temp table explicitly instead.
order_cursor with OPEN/FETCH NEXT iterates Sales.Orders row by row for work that can be expressed set-wise.
The WHILE @Counter <= 1 loop performs iterative processing instead of a set-based operation.
@Sql is built by concatenating CONVERT(nvarchar(20), @CustomerID) into the command text rather than binding the value as a parameter.
sys.sp_executesql executes @Sql with the OrderID value embedded in the text; no @params definition is supplied, so the plan is not parameterized or reusable.
#Scratch is explicitly created but never dropped before the procedure ends, leaving the temporary object alive until scope exit.
The CATCH block only selects ERROR_MESSAGE(); it neither rethrows with THROW nor returns a failure status, so callers see the procedure as successful.
RAISERROR is used for the negative-order-ID error path; THROW should be used for new error handling to preserve error semantics.
PRINT output is buffered and unstructured, making it unsuitable for reliable diagnostics.
CustomerID = 1 embeds a business identifier directly in the query instead of accepting it as a parameter or looking it up.
The unlabelled constant '20160101' is embedded in the OrderDate filter with no indication of its business meaning.
CONVERT(date, '01/02/2016') omits the style argument, so the result depends on session language/DATEFORMAT (Jan 2 vs Feb 1).
COALESCE(o.CustomerID, 0) = COALESCE(i.CustomerID, 0) wraps both join keys, inhibiting normal join optimization and matching NULL customers to each other.
Sales.Orders is joined to itself on OrderID = OrderID only to return o.OrderID, information already available from the same row.
ORDER BY o.Comments sorts on an nvarchar(max) column, forcing a wide and expensive sort over all orders.
SUM(ol.Quantity) aggregates the entire fact-like Sales.OrderLines table with no restrictive filter.
HAVING ol.OrderID > 0 is a row-level predicate applied after grouping; it belongs in WHERE so rows are filtered before aggregation.
ORDER BY OrderCount sorts the result of a scalar COUNT(*) aggregate with no GROUP BY, which is guaranteed to be a single row.
MERGE into Sales.Orders has documented concurrency and correctness edge cases; use separate IF EXISTS / UPDATE / INSERT logic.
SET Comments = Comments writes the current value back, generating log records and locks without changing any data.
DELETE filters on Quantity = -1, a broad non-key business value that can match many OrderLines rows and take wide locks.
WAITFOR DELAY '00:00:01' intentionally blocks a worker thread instead of using asynchronous scheduling.
BEGIN TRANSACTION is issued outside a TRY/CATCH boundary, so a run-time error can leave the transaction open with no rollback path.
SET IDENTITY_INSERT Sales.Orders ON changes session/table state and introduces fragile identity-management coupling.
EXEC sp_who invokes a system routine without a schema qualifier (sys.sp_who), adding name-resolution overhead and ambiguity.
SET ROWCOUNT 1 is never reset to 0, so all subsequent statements in the session, including later UPDATE/DELETE calls, are silently limited to one row.
INSERT INTO #DemoCategories VALUES (...) omits an explicit column list, so the insert breaks or misassigns values if the table's column order changes.
LIKE '%' + @CustomerName + '%' begins with a wildcard, forcing a scan of Sales.Customers for the name filter.
@CustomerName is concatenated directly into the dynamic SELECT string, allowing a caller to inject arbitrary SQL that is then executed.
sp_executesql runs @Sql with the customer name embedded in the text and no @params definition, so the input is not bound as a parameter.
sp_executesql is called without the sys schema qualifier.
UPDATE #DemoCustomers SET CustomerCategoryID = 1 has no WHERE clause and rewrites every row in the table.
The WHERE predicate on o.OrderDate filters the LEFT-joined Sales.Orders rows, removing NULL-extended rows and effectively converting the outer join to an inner join.
The unlabelled date constant '2016-01-01' is embedded in the OrderDate filter without explaining its business meaning.
DeliveryMethodID = NULL never evaluates to true, so the query always returns zero rows; use IS NULL instead.
dbo.GetCustomerType(CustomerID) in the select list forces row-by-row scalar UDF evaluation over Sales.Customers and inhibits parallelism on older versions.
The CATCH block handles the error without rolling back the transaction opened at line 238, leaving an open transaction and its locks as the procedure continues.
The CATCH block only selects ERROR_MESSAGE(); it neither rethrows nor signals failure, so callers cannot detect the failed DELETE.
WITH (INDEX = 1) hard-codes an index ID on Sales.Customers, overriding the optimizer and breaking if the index is dropped or rebuilt.
Four levels of nested derived tables (t1/t2/t3) obscure the query logic; refactor into a CTE or a single flat query.
LIKE '%A%' starts with a wildcard, so the innermost CustomerName filter scans Sales.Customers.
SELECT * from dbo.GetCustomerOrdersMulti couples callers to the function's entire output schema instead of naming required columns.
dbo.GetCustomerOrdersMulti is a multi-statement table-valued function, optimized as a black box with poor cardinality estimates; an inline TVF would be folded into the outer query.
